The medial consonant cluster of the word also get stressed /ɡʰoꞋtlai/ ‘to stir/shake’ /piꞋtʰli/ ‘rice flour’ ... /haꞋkle/ ‘early’. The di- syllabic words usually get stressed /Ꞌʧ͡orok/ ‘thunder’ /Ꞌmaraŋ/ ‘poultice’ /Ꞌlawaj/ ‘talkative’. The tri-syllabic words stress on the second to last syllable /limliꞋmɯ/ ‘smooth /majraꞋtʰi/ ‘midnight’ /aliꞋkʰoŋ/ ‘a kind of bird’ /aꞋdidar/ ‘landowner’ /balukꞋʤ͡or/ ‘malaria’ /bʰiturꞋni/ ‘inside’ ... /bisiꞋbʰat/ ‘steamed rice’ [pp.140-141]. ... new_statements.relation_note: new: nothing on record (Hajong has no catalog record and no stress statement held by the project). First usable statement: stress non-distinctive; placement described by word shape but internally inconsistent between prose (penultimate in trisyllables, initial in disyllables) and the stress marks in the examples (mostly before the final syllable). A stager should record 'predictable, non-phonemic stress; placement unclear in the source (penult per prose, final per most transcriptions)' rather than a fixed position.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in Hajong (Doskahania variety, Goalpara) is described as non-distinctive (not phonemic). Placement is given by word shape: monosyllables stressed; plain disyllables 'usually' stressed with the mark on the first syllable (/Ꞌʧ͡orok/); disyllables with a medial consonant cluster carry the mark before the cluster (/piꞋtʰli/, 'the medial consonant cluster.. get stressed'); trisyllables are said in prose to be stressed on the second-to-last syllable, but in 8 of the 9 transcribed examples the stress mark stands before the FINAL syllable (/majraꞋtʰi/, /bʰiturꞋni/, /kʰolaꞋʧ͡aŋ/), only /aꞋdidar/ showing a penult mark under the IPA convention. So the prose (penult) and the transcriptions (final, or penult only if the author writes the mark after the stressed syllable) do not agree; the only firm statement is that stress is predictable/non-contrastive. Vowel length and nasalization are also stated to be non-phonemic; intonation (rising/falling) is treated as the distinctive suprasegmental.
new_statements.exceptions: disyllables with a medial consonant cluster are singled out (stress mark before the cluster, e.g. /ɡʰoꞋtlai/, /aꞋklai/); 'usually' for disyllables; no loanword or morphological exceptions given
new_statements.identity_note: Narzary 2022/2023 describes the Doskahania (Doskahini) variety of Hajong spoken in Goalpara district, Assam (12 informants from Sesapani, Patpara and nearby villages, plus Goalpara and Dudhnoi towns). Choudhury 2015 describes Hajong as spoken in Assam generally, noting susong vs dashkahani dialect alternations (/s/~/h/). Both are the mainstream Hajong of hajo1238, not the Banai or Dalu varieties.

readall_conflicts: No catalog record or prior statement exists for Hajong, so there is no disagreement with the catalog. Between the two theses: Choudhury 2015 (Assam University; Hajong of Assam, susong and dashkahani dialects mentioned) treats segmental phonology only and states merely that tone was not found and vowel length is not contrastive; Narzary 2022/2023 (University of Hyderabad; Doskahania variety, Goalpara) adds a half-page stress section stating that stress is not distinctive and giving placement by word shape, but its prose ('tri-syllabic words stress on the second to last syllable') conflicts with its own transcriptions, where the stress mark precedes the final syllable in 8 of 9 trisyllabic examples and precedes the cluster-initial second syllable in disyllables with a medial cluster, while plain disyllables carry an initial mark. The internal inconsistency, not a clash between sources, is why the overall reading is 'unclear or contradictory' (firm part: non-phonemic, predictable stress; placement penult-per-prose vs final-per-marks).
